title: publish-release.sh's registry-visibility gate has no test for its permanent-exhaustion die() path
description:
LCLI-502 moved the registry-visibility poll (wait_for_all_visible, originally
LCLI-460) to gate the root-wrapper publish, and added a regression test proving
the gate correctly WAITS when a platform package's visibility is merely delayed
(resolves within the shared REGISTRY_WINDOW_SECONDS window). Found during that
PR's review (independently verified, not blocking the fix itself): neither that
new test nor any pre-existing test exercises the OTHER branch -- a platform
package that never becomes visible at all within the window, which hits the
die() at the end of wait_for_all_visible and aborts the whole publish.

This branch predates LCLI-502 (it's the original LCLI-460 poll's timeout path)
and was already untested before that PR landed, so this is not a regression --
but it is the single most safety-critical failure path in a script that
performs real, irreversible npm publishes, and it has zero test coverage on
either side of the change.

Also worth a one-line note from the same review: LCLI-502's AC (index 1)
required the staged-vs-missing distinction be made "by something other than
the publisher's own read." What shipped is a proof that the specific silent-
stage-under-plain-publish scenario is structurally unreachable via this
script's own npm call pattern, plus a defensive text-scan of the publish
command's own captured output (still, literally, the publisher's own read).
The reviewer called marking that AC checked "generous against its literal
wording" though not a functional defect. Not re-opening LCLI-502 for it; noting
here so a future reader of either task has the full picture.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A test exercises the case where a platform package never becomes visible within REGISTRY_WINDOW_SECONDS (or an injected shorter window for test purposes), and asserts the root wrapper is never published
The test asserts the die() message actually fires with its documented not-proof-of-failure wording, not just that the script exits non-zero
